\chapter{Family, and the Oldest Words We Have}
\label{ch:family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the four closest family members in French, each with its article, and use one sound-law to recognise their English cousins.}

Four words — père, mère, frère, sœur — and every one of them is older than Latin. Each also hands you an English word you already knew: paternal, maternal, fraternal, sorority. One sound-law, Grimm's p$\to$f and t$\to$th, turns père into father and frāter into brother in a single move, and the fused letter œ arrives here and waits in cœur, œuf and œil.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[le père]{le père — father}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-pere}



\begin{quote}
The calendar took you back two thousand years, to Rome. This word goes back further than Rome — further than Latin, further than any written language at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{e-grave} — the \textbf{è} is open, the mouth wider than for \textbf{é}. Think of the \emph{e} in English \emph{bed}, held a moment longer.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — the \textbf{r} is the French one, made at the back of the throat.
  \item Together: \textbf{le père} = \emph{luh PEHR}, one syllable after the article.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{père} is Latin \textbf{pater}, worn down by French mouths for fifteen centuries until only four letters were left.

\emph{pater} itself is inherited, not invented. Behind it stands Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r} — a word nobody ever wrote down, reconstructed from the shapes its descendants kept. Sanskrit \emph{pitṛ́}, Greek \emph{pat\'{\={e}}r}, Latin \emph{pater}: the same word, spoken across a continent, for longer than anyone can document.

English never borrowed \emph{père}, but it borrowed \emph{pater} itself, over and over, and left it visible every time:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pat}ernal, \textbf{pat}ernity — \textquotedblleft{}of a father\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{pat}ron — a man who stands to you as a father would
  \item \textbf{pat}riarch, ex\textbf{pat}riate, \textbf{pat}rimony
\end{itemize}

So the French word is short and the English cousins are long, and they are the same word. When \emph{père} looks like nothing you know, say \emph{paternal} and the \emph{p} and the \emph{t} are still there.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le père\textquotedblright{} — \emph{luh PEHR}, the \textbf{è} open and the \textbf{r} in the throat
  \item the ladder — \textquotedblleft{}*ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r, pater, père\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}père $\to$ paternal, patron\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{p} and \emph{t} still standing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the father\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{le père}, \emph{luh PEHR}.) Which article does it take, and what does that tell you? (\textbf{le} — it is masculine.) What Latin word is it? (\textbf{pater}.) Name two English words with that \emph{pater} still inside them. (\textbf{paternal}, \textbf{patron} — also \emph{paternity}, \emph{patriarch}.) Next: the other half of the pair.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la mère]{la mère — mother}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-mere}



\begin{quote}
The same word, one letter different, one article different — and a much stranger set of English cousins waiting at the end of it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{la mère} = \emph{lah MEHR}. The vowel is the identical open \textbf{è} you just met in \textbf{père}; only the first consonant changes.
  \item Say them back to back — \emph{père, mère} — and hear that the rhyme is exact. That rhyme is not a coincidence; it is two inherited words worn down by the same mouths in the same way.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mère} is Latin \textbf{māter}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*méh\textsubscript{2}tēr}.

The obvious English cousins are the ones you would guess:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{mat}ernal, \textbf{mat}ernity — \textquotedblleft{}of a mother\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{mat}ron, \textbf{mat}riarch, alma \textbf{mat}er
\end{itemize}

And then there is one nobody guesses. Latin took \emph{māter} and built \textbf{materia} from it — originally the \textbf{usable wood of a tree}, the growing part, the stuff a mother-trunk yields. Roman writers then stretched \emph{materia} to mean the stuff anything is made of, and English inherited it twice over:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{material} — what a thing is made of
  \item \textbf{matter} — stuff itself, the physical world
\end{itemize}

So when a physicist says \emph{matter}, the word underneath is \emph{mother}. That is the kind of thing etymology is for: not a party trick, but a reminder that abstract vocabulary is almost always a concrete word that travelled.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la mère\textquotedblright{} — \emph{lah MEHR}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}le père, la mère\textquotedblright{}; the rhyme is exact, the articles are not
  \item the surprising one — \textquotedblleft{}māter $\to$ materia $\to$ matter\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the mother\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{la mère}, \emph{lah MEHR}.) Which article, and why is it not the same as \emph{père}'s? (\textbf{la} — \emph{mère} is feminine.) Give both parents together. (\textbf{le père, la mère}.) Which everyday English word for physical stuff comes from \emph{māter}? (\textbf{matter} — through \emph{materia}, the wood a tree yields.) Next: why English says \emph{father} where French says \emph{père}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[père / father]{père / father — one sound-law}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-grimm}



\begin{quote}
You have met two words that mean what English \emph{father} and \emph{mother} mean, and look almost nothing like them. That is about to stop being true.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same word went down two roads}]
French took \emph{pater} and \emph{māter} straight from Latin. English did \textbf{not} borrow them from anybody. It inherited the very same Proto-Indo-European words down a different branch of the family — and on that branch, one systematic change hit every word at once. It is called \textbf{Grimm's law}, and the part that matters here is short: \textbf{p became f, and t became th.}

Apply it and watch the disguise fall off. Each row is one inherited word, shown first as it is reconstructed, then down each of the two roads:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Proto-Indo-European} & \textbf{Latin $\to$ French} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
{*}ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r & \emph{pater} $\to$ \textbf{père} & \textbf{f}a\textbf{th}er \\
{*}méh\textsubscript{2}tēr & \emph{māter} $\to$ \textbf{mère} & \textbf{m}o\textbf{th}er \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{père} keeps the \textbf{p}; \emph{father} shifts it to \textbf{f}. The \emph{t} of \emph{pater} is still a \emph{t} in French and has become \emph{th} in English. Nothing else moved.

This is why the resemblance between \emph{maternal} and \emph{mother} feels different from the resemblance between \emph{paternal} and \emph{father}: \textbf{maternal} came into English late, borrowed whole from Latin with its \emph{t} intact, while \textbf{mother} came down the long way and took the sound-change with it. Two arrivals of one word, centuries apart.

The point is not the pair. It is that sound-change is \textbf{regular} — it applies to a language wholesale, not word by word — which is exactly what makes a word you have never seen guessable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the law — \textquotedblleft{}p becomes f, t becomes th\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}père, father\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}mère, mother\textquotedblright{}; hear the same word twice
  \item the two arrivals — \textquotedblleft{}maternal came by boat, mother came on foot\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two sounds does Grimm's law change, in the version you need here? (\textbf{p $\to$ f} and \textbf{t $\to$ th}.) Are \emph{père} and \emph{father} borrowed from each other? (\textbf{No} — they are the \textbf{same inherited word}, arriving by two different roads.) Why does \emph{maternal} keep its \emph{t} while \emph{mother} does not? (\emph{maternal} was \textbf{borrowed late from Latin}; \emph{mother} came down the Germanic road and took the sound-change.) Next: the brother.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le frère]{le frère — brother}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-frere}



\begin{quote}
Parents done. The next word rhymes with both of them, and it lets you use the sound-law you just learned instead of only hearing about it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{le frère} = \emph{luh FREHR}. The same open \textbf{è}, the same throat \textbf{r} — and now an \textbf{r} on each side of the vowel, which is the only hard part.
  \item Say \textbf{père}, then \textbf{frère}. One consonant has been added at the front; everything else is identical.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{frère} is Latin \textbf{frāter}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}.

Now use what you have. English \textbf{brother} is that same PIE word down the Germanic road: the \emph{t} became \emph{th}, exactly as it did in \emph{father} and \emph{mother}. The law you just met explains a third pair without being told to.

By the Latin road, English got the formal set:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{frat}ernal, \textbf{frat}ernity, \textbf{frat}ernize
  \item and, softened through Old French \emph{frere}, \textbf{friar} — a monk who is literally a \emph{brother} of his order
\end{itemize}

\emph{Fraternity} and \emph{friar} are the same word twice, once in a lecture hall and once in a monastery, and the difference between them is only how long each spent in a French mouth on the way.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le frère\textquotedblright{} — \emph{luh FREHR}, an \emph{r} on both sides of the vowel
  \item the three so far — \textquotedblleft{}le père, la mère, le frère\textquotedblright{}
  \item the law again — \textquotedblleft{}frāter, brother: the \emph{t} went to \emph{th}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}frère $\to$ fraternal, friar\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the brother\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{le frère}, \emph{luh FREHR}.) What Latin word is behind it? (\textbf{frāter}.) Which sound-change turns \emph{frāter} into English \emph{brother}? (The same one: \textbf{t $\to$ th}.) What is a \textbf{friar}, underneath the word? (A \textbf{brother} — the same \emph{frère}, worn down through Old French.) Next: the sister, and a letter you have not met.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sœur]{la sœur — sister}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-soeur}



\begin{quote}
Three words that rhyme, and then this one. \emph{Père, mère, frère} — and \textbf{sœur}, which refuses the pattern and brings a letter with it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{la sœur} = \emph{lah SUR}, but not the \emph{sur} of English \emph{sure}. Round your lips as if to say \emph{oo}, then say \emph{eh} without moving them. That rounded front vowel is what \textbf{œu} spells.
  \item The \textbf{r} is the throat \textbf{r}, as in the other three.
  \item The strange letter is \textbf{œ}, an \emph{o} and an \emph{e} fused into one. It gets a lesson of its own next; for now, read it as the single vowel you just made.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sœur} is Latin \textbf{soror} — and you can watch it collapse:

\emph{soror} $\to$ \emph{seror} $\to$ \emph{suer} $\to$ \textbf{sœur}

Two syllables ground down into one, which is why it stopped rhyming with its three relatives. They were worn evenly; this one was worn out of shape.

English kept \emph{soror} whole in the borrowed words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{soror}ity, \textbf{soror}al
  \item and a nun is still addressed as \textbf{Sister} in English and \textbf{ma sœur} in French, the same word in both mouths
\end{itemize}

English \textbf{sister} is not from \emph{soror} by borrowing — it comes down the Germanic road from the same PIE \textbf{*swésōr}. So \emph{soror} and \emph{sister} are cousins who have not spoken since before either language existed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la sœur\textquotedblright{} — lips rounded, then \emph{eh} without moving them
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}le frère, la sœur\textquotedblright{}
  \item the collapse — \textquotedblleft{}soror, seror, sœur\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}the sister\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{la sœur}, \emph{lah SUR} with rounded lips.) What Latin word is behind it? (\textbf{soror}.) Why does it not rhyme with the other three? (It was worn down from \textbf{two syllables to one} — \emph{soror} $\to$ \emph{sœur}.) An English word that kept \emph{soror} whole? (\textbf{sorority}.) Next: that fused letter, on its own.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[œ]{œ — one letter, not two}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-oe}



\begin{quote}
You have just read a word containing a character English does not own. It is worth two minutes on its own, because it is not decoration and it is not rare.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: œ, one letter and not two}
\textbf{œ} is an \emph{o} and an \emph{e} pushed together into a \textbf{single letter}. French calls it \emph{e dans l'o} — \textquotedblleft{}e in the o\textquotedblright{} — which is exactly what it looks like.

Three things follow, and they are the whole lesson:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item It counts as \textbf{one} letter when you spell aloud. \textbf{sœur} is spelled \emph{s-œ-u-r}: four letters, not five.
  \item Writing it as two separate letters — \emph{soeur} — is a \textbf{substitution}, the way writing \emph{ae} for \emph{æ} is. French readers accept it and French typography does not; a printed book, a newspaper and a road sign all use \textbf{œ}.
  \item It is not a separate sound of its own. In \textbf{sœur} the vowel is spelled \textbf{œu}, the rounded vowel you made in the last lesson.
\end{itemize}

Its capital exists too, and looks like what you would expect: \textbf{Œ}.

\subsection*{Writing: œ, and the four words that need it}
The list of everyday \textbf{œ} words is short enough to hold in your head, and you already have one of them:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{la sœur} — the sister, which you have
  \item \textbf{le cœur} — the heart
  \item \textbf{l'œuf} — the egg
  \item \textbf{l'œil} — the eye
\end{itemize}

\textbf{l'œuf} and \textbf{l'œil} both come back later in this book as words in their own right, so learning the letter now means that when they arrive, only the meaning is new. \textbf{le cœur} is here because you will meet it everywhere else — it is one of the most common nouns in the language — and because four words is a short enough list to simply keep.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the name of the letter — \textquotedblleft{}e dans l'o\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} spell it — \textquotedblleft{}s-œ-u-r\textquotedblright{}, four letters
  \item \emph{Say it:} the short list — \textquotedblleft{}sœur, cœur, œuf, œil\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{œ} three times: draw the \emph{o}, then start the \emph{e} inside its right edge
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many letters is \textbf{œ}? (\textbf{One.}) What does French call it? (\emph{e dans l'o} — \textquotedblleft{}e in the o\textquotedblright{}.) How many letters in \textbf{sœur}? (\textbf{Four} — \emph{s-œ-u-r}.) Name two other words that use it. (\textbf{cœur}, \textbf{œuf}, \textbf{œil} — any two.) Next: putting the family together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — four words, one law}

\label{lesson:FR-C10-practice}



\begin{quote}
Four words, learned one at a time. Run them as a set now, and then cash in what each one buys you in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the set, with articles}
The article is half the word, and a family word said bare is a word half learned.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le père, la mère\textquotedblright{} — the parents, masculine then feminine
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le frère, la sœur\textquotedblright{} — the siblings, same order
  \item all four straight through, then in reverse
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: the three that rhyme, and the one that does not}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}père, mère, frère\textquotedblright{} — one vowel, three times: the open \textbf{è}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sœur\textquotedblright{} after them, and hear the break
  \item why it broke — \textquotedblleft{}soror ground down two syllables into one\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: cash in the English}
Each French word hands you an English one you already knew and never thought about, and the French is the key rather than the lock.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}père $\to$ paternal, patron\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mère $\to$ maternal, matter\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}frère $\to$ fraternal, friar\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sœur $\to$ sorority\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{four family words}, each with its article.
  \item \textbf{one sound-law} — Grimm's law, \emph{p $\to$ f} and \emph{t $\to$ th}. It is why \emph{père} is \emph{father}, \emph{mère} is \emph{mother} and \emph{frāter} is \emph{brother}, and it turned three separate memorisations into one fact.
  \item \textbf{a letter} — \textbf{œ}, one character, waiting in \emph{cœur}, \emph{œuf} and \emph{œil}.
  \item \textbf{a habit worth more than any of them}: when a French word looks like nothing, reach for the long formal English word rather than the short common one. \emph{Père} is opaque next to \emph{father} and obvious next to \emph{paternal}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all four family words with their articles. (\textbf{le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur}.) Which two are feminine? (\textbf{la mère, la sœur}.) State Grimm's law in the form you need. (\textbf{p $\to$ f}, \textbf{t $\to$ th}.) Use it: what English word is \emph{frāter}? (\textbf{brother}.) How many letters is \textbf{œ}, and name a word besides \emph{sœur} that has it. (\textbf{One}; \emph{cœur}, \emph{œuf} or \emph{œil}.) Which English word for physical stuff traces back to \emph{mère}? (\textbf{matter}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
